sourceInformation.genre: Shooter: on-rails action-adventure with rail movement, stop-and-scan first-person aiming, persona switching and boss fights
sourceInformation.perspective: Third person: fixed cinematic rail cameras with hard cuts while moving; first person while aiming
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.2 (2D engine and its 3D module, from the handoff at commit 4390a98); three.js r182 and Rapier 0.19.3 from jsDelivr; AI Hub session client 1.4.0, unmodified; Node 24 and Playwright 1.63.0 for tests
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's native pixel look (PS1 resolution, card-drawn Humanoid rigs), flat shading, procedural textures and pen-drawn props; no image files
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's procedural Humanoid rig (poses, run, aim, down); no new move set
sourceInformation.audio: The engine's chip synth: sound effects, songs written as note strings, laughter as arpeggio voices, Animalese-style dialogue blips; no audio files
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, ghost mode: the Echo Run reports its time and progress to the hub
sourceInformation.testing: Node rule tests of the sim and headless Chromium flows, behind one command (node tests/run.mjs); bot playthroughs of every area; seeded and repeatable
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux (WSL2); headless Chromium 1243 via Playwright 1.63.0, WebGL 2 under SwiftShader

testingFeedback: About fifteen issues, by my count, from the Node sim tests, the bot playthroughs and headless Chromium runs.

Five were game-breaking: a crash opening Room 7 (the New Game path), a black frame from the Comic cel filter defaults, two Rime gates that could lock a run, and a junction that committed or stalled on its own.
The most helpful test was the Node playthrough: a bot drives each area through the sim with no page and stops at the first soft-lock, stall or crash, and seeding makes it repeatable.
The least helpful was checking single screenshots; under the software renderer, fixed-time waits in the browser flows were flaky until they polled for the expected scene.
engineFeedback: The 3D module's fixed cameras and the card-drawn rigs, with the pause menu, settings and saves coming for free.

Yes. I guessed the particle argument orders (sparks takes a direction, text takes x, y, z first), the pen box centre convention, and the cel filter options, which gave a black frame. A pause-menu item does not close the menu, so Dev Mode needed shell.hide().
The rail walker with its junctions and gates, the Whiteout AI and scan, the persona abilities, the dev panel, the bot and the test harness.
Working out the 3D API from its header without a typed reference, and the slow shader builds when a scene switches under a software renderer.
None. All changes are in the game's own src/ files; the engine files are unmodified copies.
Let a pause-menu item's callback close the menu by default, or say plainly that it must call shell.hide().
promptFeedback: The deliverables are concrete: the file name, the four report sections, the exit-interview shape and the one-command test rule.

STAGE asks me to follow PLAN.md, which is about 2,100 lines and asks for engine patches and seven full personas, while TASK sets the same feature-complete bar. The scope had to be cut to fit one session, and it was not clear which plan details were required.
Fitting the plan into one session: it describes a game several times this size, with cutscenes, NPCs, hand-drawn accessories and a long list of engine patches.
Give the plan a must, should and cut list, a size budget, and say which engine patches are optional.

aiHub.name: Skiller7
aiHub.description: An on-rails shooter in the manner of Killer7: ride the rails, stop, scan for the laughing invisible Whiteouts and shoot their warm spots, wear seven coats and melt two bosses.
aiHub.controls: W/Cross walk, S/Circle stop, A/D or R3 turn, RMB/L2 aim, LMB/R2 fire, Space/L1 scan, E/R1 ability, Q/Triangle switch, F/Square interact
